name: Pazeh-Kahabu
confidence_why: Li and Tsuchida 2001, Blust 1999 and Macaulay 2020 and 2021 all place Pazeh stress on the final syllable, and Lin 2025 finds the same default in the Kaxabu dialect, with the only differences being details, namely the extra prominence that Macaulay 2020 and 2021 find on heavy non-final syllables and the leftward pull of initial long vowels and longer words that Lin 2025 finds in Kaxabu.

new_statements.quote: In Pazeh as spoken by Adunu, words may receive one pitch accent, or they may receive two. All words receive a final pitch accent. Vowel-vowel sequences that have not undergone glide formation, that is, long vowels, [ai] and [au] sequences, receive a pitch accent. When this occurs in a non-final syllable, both this and the final syllable receive pitch accents, even if they are adjacent syllables. (p. 563) [...] While it may be argued that final stress in Pazeh is ‘primary’ in that it is always present, while non-final stress would be ‘secondary’, there is no evidence of a ‘primary’ vs. ‘secondary’ distinction in the magnitude of pitch accents. (p. 572)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress = final syllable): the dissertation states final stress/pitch accent on every word. It adds detail the catalog lacks: weight-sensitive extra prominence on non-final long-vowel/diphthong syllables, suffixes inside the stress domain, two extrametrical particles, no primary/secondary magnitude distinction, and a reported dialect difference (Kaxabu with alternating rhythmic stress per Lim 2016). Note the PDF download at academicworks.cuny.edu was blocked by an automated-access block on three tries and CORE's PDF mirror returned 404; the full text was recovered from the fullText field embedded in CORE's reader page (https://core.ac.uk/reader/382…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence (realised as a L+H*L pitch accent) always falls on the final syllable of the word; the stress domain includes suffixes, so a monosyllabic suffix takes the stress (p. 238: 'Without a suffix, stress surfaces on the final syllable of the stem. With a suffix, stress surfaces on the suffix.'). In the comparative chapter Pazeh is grouped with the ultima-prominence languages (p. 654: 'The second most common location of prominence in Formosan languages is the ultima. This is found in two areas of Taiwan: the northern mountains, including Saisiyat, Atayal, and Pazeh') and called stress-final (p. 676: 'Kavalan and Pazeh are both stress-final languages in which the postnuclear L is deleted, specifically when the syllable’s coda is voiceless.'). In addition, any non-final syllable containing a long vowel or an /ai/ /au/ sequence (including ones created by CVV- progressive reduplication or across a prefix boundary, e.g. ma-usay, laa-langui) also receives a pitch accent; syllables with codas or with glide-formed [ja] [wa] do not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-final prominence on heavy syllables (long vowel, [ai], [au]) is obligatory when available (p. 563, grids 178-181); the author declines to call it 'secondary' because pitch accents on final and non-final syllables do not differ in magnitude (p. 572). One word, aisiiyay 'resemble', has two heavy non-final syllables but only the second ([siː]) plus the ultima are accented (p. 564).
new_statements.exceptions: Two particles are optionally extrametrical: the perfect marker lia and the question marker sai; when extrametrical they bear no pitch accent and the final accent falls on the preceding word's ultima (p. 566, ex. 188-189: purehát lia, tabarák sai). Codas do not make a syllable heavy (p. 564). For the Kaxabu dialect the work reports, from H.-S. Lim (2016), a different pattern: 'while Pazeh (at least as spoken by Adunu) aligns one pitch accent to the final syllable and the rest to preceding heavy syllables, the Kaxabu word has rhythmic stress on alternating syllables' (p. 573, citing Lim 2016: 106, minaakuakux [L.H.L.H.L.H]).
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation's original data come from a single speaker of the Pazeh dialect (Adunu, Ailan/Puli); the Kaxabu dialect is treated only through H.-S. Lim's (2016) thesis and Kunay's (2015) dictionary (§11.6, p. 572-573), and the conclusion (p. 697) states Kaxabu is 'not covered in this dissertation'. The glottocode kulo1237 covers both dialects.

tone_statements.citation: Lim, Hong-sui & Elizabeth Zeitoun. 2023. Kaxabu and Pazih. In P. J.-k. Li, E. Zeitoun & R. De Busser (eds.), Handbook of Formosan Languages: The Indigenous Languages of Taiwan (Brill's Handbooks in Linguistics 5). Leiden: Brill.
tone_statements.quote: In contrast to Pazeh, pitch in Kaxabu is intrinsically related to stress, perhaps as a result of language contact. In Kaxabu, the stressed syllable has a high pitch (henceforth H). It follows a low pitch if the word is disyllabic, e.g., punu ‘head’ (L.H), or a mid pitch (M) if the word is trisyllabic, as in tulala ‘flower’ (L.M.H). ... If a word contains a heavy syllable in initial position, the first syllable is H rather than L. In disyllabic words, the pitch is H.H, as in dauik ‘eye’.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 51.2.3 'Syllable Structure, Stress, and Intonation', chapter pp. 7-8
tone_statements.summary: Final stress in both dialects. Kaxabu word pitch (H on stressed final, L/M before, H if initial heavy) is presented as tied to stress, not lexical tone; 'tone' never used; Pazeh pitch not described.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement with the catalog: Macaulay 2021 places obligatory word prominence on the final syllable of Pazeh, matching the catalog's final-stress rule. The only tension is dialect-internal and is reported, not observed, by the work: Pazeh (Adunu) has final accent plus extra accents on heavy non-final syllables, whereas Kaxabu is said (after H.-S. Lim 2016) to have rhythmic stress on alternating syllables (p. 573); both dialects still have prominence on the ultima, so the catalog's final-stress reading stands for the language as a whole, but a weight-sensitive or rhythmic refinement of the non-final pattern would be defensible.
